m.s: The Fall of the Walls of Jericho
o: Eternal God, thank you for letting me see the beginning of a new day. I acknowledge that you are the one who sustains my life and that every morning is a sign of your mercy. Place me in your hands today and teach me to walk according to your will and not according to my fears.

Lord, sometimes I find myself before walls that seem impossible: problems that will not resolve, wounded relationships, habits I cannot manage to change. Like Israel before Jericho, I do not have the strength to bring them down by myself. But you told Joshua that you had given the city into his hands. Give me the faith to believe that what you promise, you fulfill, and the patience to obey even when your ways seem strange to me. Thank you, Lord, because you never tire of sustaining me, and because your faithfulness is greater than any obstacle I will meet today.

Help me to be steady in what you ask of me today, even if it seems small. May I not be discouraged if I do not see results right away. May my trust rest not on what I see, but on who you are. Keep my steps, bless my work, and give me a heart willing to serve others with joy. May I remember today that victory comes from you and not from my own strength. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: After crossing the Jordan, the people of Israel found themselves before Jericho, a closed and fortified city. The Bible says that its gates were tightly shut because of the Israelites, and that no one went out or came in. Humanly speaking, there was no way to take it.

Then God gave Joshua a plan unlike any battle plan. For six days the men of war were to march around the city once a day, and seven priests would carry trumpets of ram's horns before the ark. On the seventh day, they would march around the city seven times, and the priests would blow the trumpets. When they heard the long blast, all the people were to shout a great shout, and the wall of the city would fall down.

Imagine what it must have been like to walk in silence around those walls, day after day, without seeing any change. But the people obeyed. On the seventh day, after the seventh circuit, Joshua told the people to shout, for the LORD had given them the city. The people shouted, the trumpets sounded, and the wall fell down, so that everyone went straight up into the city and they captured it.

Before the conquest, near the city, Joshua had been visited by a man with a drawn sword in his hand, who introduced himself as the commander of the army of the LORD. Joshua fell facedown to the ground and worshiped, and he was told to take off his sandals, for the place was holy. The battle belonged to the Lord.

The book of Hebrews sums up this story in one short sentence: by faith the walls of Jericho fell, after they had been encircled for seven days. They did not fall by the strength of the army, but by the faith that obeys what God had said.
m.c: May you walk today with the confidence that God goes before you. Every step of obedience, even the smallest, is in his hands. Go out with courage, for the Lord is faithful and cares for you in everything you do.
m: Jericho teaches us that God does not always act the way we expect. An army would have attacked with ladders and battering rams, but God asked them to walk, to wait, and to trust. Sometimes the hardest part of faith is not action, but obedient waiting when you see no results.

Think about the people during those six days. Every lap around the city seemed to change nothing. The walls stayed just as high. And yet every step counted. It is the same with many good things in our lives: praying for a family member, persevering in honest work, forgiving little by little, being consistent in caring for our children. It seems as if nothing is happening, but God is at work.

Today you may ask yourself what your wall is. Perhaps a debt, an illness, a family situation, or a fear that has been with you for a long time. You do not have to bring it down with your own strength. Your part is to obey what God shows you: pray, speak sincerely, do what is right, take the next step, and wait in faith.

And remember that the people also shouted. When God's time came, they expressed their faith with joy. Today, instead of complaining about what is lacking, give thanks for what God has already done and declare with your mouth that he is faithful. Obedient and grateful faith is the faith that sees walls fall in their time. This same spirit can go with you all week long: patient obedience, steady trust, and sincere gratitude.

t.s: Elisha and the Heavenly Army at Dothan
o: Good Father, at the end of this day, I come to you with a grateful heart. Thank you for keeping me, for providing what I needed, and for every moment when I felt your kindness, even if I did not recognize it at the time. Your faithfulness has accompanied me from morning to evening.

I confess that today there were moments when I looked only at what was in front of me and let fear carry me away. Open the eyes of my heart, Lord, as you opened the eyes of Elisha's servant, to see that those who are with me are more than those who are against me. I cast all my anxiety on you, because you care for me. I hand over to you my unfinished tasks, my worries about tomorrow, and the things I cannot control. Thank you for the people who helped me today, for the small joys I sometimes let slip by, and for the fact that your love does not depend on my successes.

Take care of my family while we sleep and watch over our homes. Heal what is sick, comfort those who weep, and strengthen those who feel alone. Give me deep sleep and a hope-filled awakening. Thank you, because you never leave me nor forsake me. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: Elisha was a prophet in Israel, and God often revealed to him the plans of the king of Syria when he set ambushes against Israel. The king of Syria, furious, discovered that it was the prophet who was warning them, and he sent horses, chariots, and a great army to the city of Dothan, where Elisha was. They arrived by night and surrounded the city.

When Elisha's servant got up early in the morning and went out, he saw the army with its horses and chariots all around the city. Terrified, he ran to tell his master: Alas, my lord! What shall we do? Humanly speaking, the situation was hopeless.

Elisha answered calmly: Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them. And he prayed: LORD, open his eyes, that he may see. The Lord opened the servant's eyes, and he saw that the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.

When the servant's eyes were opened, fear gave way to calm. This story, written in the second book of Kings, has comforted believers for centuries, because it reminds us that the one who is in danger is not alone. God's presence is real even if our eyes do not always perceive it, and his resources exceed every threat we face. God cares for his people in ways we cannot even imagine.

What changed was not the visible situation, but the servant's ability to see the whole reality. God had been present with his protection all along. From the beginning, the heavenly army surrounded the prophet, and this young man only needed God to open his eyes to behold it.
t.c: Rest tonight, for God watches over you with more care than you imagine. Place every burden in his hands and let his peace guard your heart. Tomorrow will find you once more with his goodness and faithfulness. May your heart fill with gratitude as you close your eyes.
m: How often we end the day exhausted because we have looked only at the army surrounding us: debts, bad news, conflicts, uncertainty. Elisha's servant was not wrong about what he saw; the Syrian army was real. His mistake was thinking that was all there was.

The Bible invites us to see further. This does not mean denying problems, but remembering that God is present too and that his protection is greater than any threat. Peter puts it simply: cast all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you. He does not say to forget the worry, but to cast it on God, like someone setting a heavy burden into stronger hands.

Tonight, do a simple exercise. Think of the situation that worries you most and, in prayer, describe it to God in your own words. Then say: Lord, open my eyes to see your goodness. Next, remember three moments from the day when God helped you, even small ones: a kind word, a door that opened, a problem that got resolved.

Finally, let go of what you cannot control. God does not ask you to solve everything before you sleep; he asks you to trust him. Lie down in peace, knowing that, as at Dothan, there is more from God on your side than what you see. And tomorrow, when you wake, begin again with gratitude.
